source_text: Ὡς δὴ σύ γε, ὦ βέλτιστε, καὶ εἰ νηῒ χειμαζομένῃ χεῖρα ὀρέγομενἢ πολιορκουμένῃ πόλει, ἢ ὑπὸ πυρὸς οἰκίᾳ δαπανωμένῃ, ἢ σκάφεσι βοηθοῦντες, ἢ φάλαγξιν, ἢ σβεστηρίοις ὀργάνοις, πάντως ἂν ἢ καταποντιστὰς ἡμᾶς ὠνόμασας, ἢ τῆς πόλεως, ἢ τῆς οἰκίας ἐραστὰς, ἀλλ' οὐ προστάτας καὶ κηδε μόνας. Ζʹ. Ἀλλ' οὐχ οὕτω, φησὶ, δοκεῖ τοῖς πολλοῖς. Τί δέ μοι διαφέρει, ᾧ τοῦ εἶναι πλεῖον ὁ λόγος, μᾶλλον δὲ πᾶς; Τοῦτο γὰρ, ἢ κατέκρινεν, ἢ ἐδικαίωσεν· ἢ ἄθλιον πεποίηκεν, ἢ μακάριον. Τὸ δὲ δο κεῖν, οὐδὲν πρὸς ἡμᾶς, ὤσπερ οὐδὲ ὄναρ ἀλλότριον. Οὐχ οὕτω, φησὶ, δοκεῖς τοῖς πολλοῖς, ἄνθρωπε. Ἡ γῆ δὲ δοκεῖ τοῖς ἰλιγγιῶσιν ἑστάναι; τοῖς δὲ μεθύουσι νήφειν οἱ νήφοντες, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐπὶ κεφαλὴν βαδίζειν, ἢ περιτρέπεσθαι; τὸ μέλι δὲ, οὐ πικρόν ἐστιν, ὅτε καὶ οἷς νομίζεται, νοσοῦσί τε καὶ κακῶς διακει μένοις; Ἀλλ' οὐ παρὰ τοῦτο τὰ πράγματα οὕτως ἔχει, ὡς δοκεῖ τοῖς πάσχουσιν. Δεῖξον οὖν ὑγιαίνον τας τοὺς οὕτως ὑπειληφότας, καὶ τότε ἡμῖν παραί νεσον μετατίθεσθαι· ἢ καταγίνωσκε, μὴ πειθο μένων, ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τῆς αὐτῆς ἱσταμένων κρίσεως. Οὐχ οὕτω δοκῶ τοῖς πολλοῖς, Θεῷ δὲ οὕτω· καὶ οὐ δοκῶ, πεφανέρωμαι δὲ τῷ εἰδότι τὰ πάντα πρὶν γενέ σεως αὐτῶν, τῷ πλάσσοντι καταμόνας τὰς καρ δίας ἡμῶν, τῷ συνιέντι εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔργα ἡμῶν, τὰ κινήματα, καὶ τὰ διανοήματα, μεθ' ὧν τὰ πραττόμενα, ὃν λανθάνει τῶν ὄντων οὐδὲν, οὐδὲ λαθεῖν δύ ναται, ὃς ἑτέρως ὁρᾷ τὰ ἡμέτερα, ἢ ὡς ὁρῶσιν ἄν θρωποι. Ἄνθρωπος μὲν γὰρ εἰς πρόσωπον, ὁ δὲ Θεὸς εἰς καρδίαν. Ἤκουσας τῆς Γραφῆς λεγού σης, καὶ πίστευε. Οὗ φροντιστέον μᾶλλον, ἢ πάντων ὁμοῦ τῶν ἄλλων, τοῖς γε νοῦν ἔχουσιν. Ἢ δύο μὲν ἀνθρώποις περὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ πράγματος συμβούλοις χρώμενος, συνετωτέρῳ τε καὶ ἀμαθεστέρῳ, οὐκ ἂν εὖ φρονεῖν ἔδοξας, εἰ τὸν συνετώτερον παρεὶς, τῷ ἀμαθεστέρῳ κατηκολούθησας; οὐδὲ γὰρ ὁ Ῥοβοὰμ ἐπῃνέθη, ὅτι τὴν βουλὴν τῶν πρεσβυτέρων ἀτιμάσας, τὴν τῶν νεωτέρων ἔστησε. Θεοῦ δὲ καὶ ἀνθρώ πων ἐξεταζομένων, προτιμήσεις τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων; Οὐ σύ γε, ἂν ἐμοὶ πείθῃ, καὶ φρονῇς ἄμεινον. Ηʹ. Ἀλλ' αἰσχυνόμεθά σου, φησὶ, ταῖς ὕβρεσιν. Ἐγὼ δὲ ὑμῖν, ὅτι αἰσχύνεσθε. Εἰ μὲν γὰρ ὀρθῶς ταῦτα πάσχομεν, αἰσχυντέον ἡμῖν μᾶλλον, ἢ ὑμῖν ἐφ' ἡμῖν· οὐχ ὅτι ἀτιμαζόμεθα μᾶλλον, ἢ ὅτι ἐσμὲν ἀτιμίας ἄξιοι· εἰ δὲ ἀδίκως, τῶν ὑβριζόντων τὸ ἔγκλη-μα, καὶ ὑπὲρ ἐκείνων μᾶλλον, ἢ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀγα-νακτητέον· ἐκεῖνοι γὰρ οἱ κακῶς πάσχοντες. Εἰ δέ με ὄντα κακὸν, ἄριστον ὑπελάμβανες, τί με ποιεῖν ἐχρῆν; Εἶναι μᾶλλον κακὸν, ἵνα πλέον ἀρέσκω σοί; Οὐκ ἂν τοῦτο ἐμαυτῷ συνεβούλευσα. Οὕτως οὐδὲ, εἰ κατορθοῦντά με πταίειν ὑπολαμβάνεις, τοῦ κατορθοῦν διὰ σὲ μεταθήσομαι. Ζῶ γὰρ, οὐ σοὶ μᾶλλον ἢ ἐμαυτῷ· καὶ σύμβουλον ἔχω περὶ πάν-των τὸν λόγον, καὶ τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ δικαιώματα, ὑφ' ὧν ἁλίσκομαι μὲν πολλάκις, οὐδενὸς κατηγοροῦντος· ἀφίεμαι δὲ, πολλῶν κατακρινόντων. Καὶ τοῦτο μό-νον οὐκ ἔστι διαφυγεῖν, τὸ ἔνδον καὶ ἐν ἡμῖν αὐτοῖς δικαστήριον, πρὸς ὃ βλέποντας μόνον, τὴν εὐθεῖαν ὁδὸν ἰτέον.
orientation: Gregory answers his opponents' objections that the many disapprove of him and that they are ashamed at the insults he suffers, as he denies desiring the see.
pass_a_gloss: So then you, O best fellow, even if we stretch out a hand to a ship tossed by storm or to a city besieged, or to a house consumed by fire, helping with small boats or with battle lines or with extinguishing instruments, in every case you would have called us either those who sink ships, or lovers of the city or of the house, but not protectors and guardians. But ‘Not so it seems to the many,’ he says. And what difference is that to me, for whom reason is more than being, or rather everything? For this either condemned or acquitted; either made wretched or blessed. But seeming is nothing to us, just as another’s dream is nothing. ‘You do not so seem to the many, fellow,’ he says. Does the earth seem to those who are dizzy to stand still? And to the drunk do the sober seem to be sober, and not to walk on head or to turn round? And honey, is it not bitter, whenever it is thought so by those who are sick and badly disposed? But things are not for this reason so as they seem to those who suffer. Show then those who supposed so to be healthy, and then advise us to change; or condemn them, when they are not persuaded but stand on the same judgment. I do not so seem to the many, but so to God; and I am not seen as seeming, but I have been made manifest to the one who knows all things before their birth, who fashions our hearts each alone, who understands toward all our works, movements, and thoughts, with which the things done are done, whom nothing of beings escapes nor can escape, who sees our things differently than as men see. For man looks to face, but God to heart. You heard Scripture saying this, and believe. This must be cared for more than all the other things together, at least by those who have mind. Or if you use two men as counselors about the same matter, both a more intelligent and a more ignorant, would you not fail to seem to think well, if you let go the more intelligent and followed the more ignorant? For neither was Rehoboam praised, because he dishonored the counsel of the elders and established that of the younger. But when God and men are weighed against each other, will you prefer the things of men? Not you, at least if you obey me and think better. But ‘We are ashamed for you because of your disgraces,’ he says. But I am ashamed for you, because you are ashamed. For if we suffer these things rightly, we must be ashamed for ourselves more than you for us; not because we are dishonored more, but because we are worthy of dishonor; but if unjustly, the charge belongs to those who insult, and one must be indignant for them more than for us; for they are the ones faring badly. But if when I was bad you supposed me best, what ought I to do? To be bad rather, so that I please you more? I would not have counseled this to myself. So neither, if when I do right you suppose me to err, shall I change from doing right because of you. For I live, not for you more than for myself; and I have as counselor about all things reason and the judgments of God, by whom I am often caught, with no one accusing, and acquitted, with many condemning. And this alone it is not possible to escape, the court within and in ourselves, looking to which alone one must go the straight way.

choices.why: Ship image requires hostile wreckers who cause sinking, answering the rescue with skiffs; keeps agent force of -της noun.

choices.term: ᾧ τοῦ εἶναι πλεῖον ὁ λόγος, μᾶλλον δὲ πᾶς
choices.english: for whom reason is more than being, or rather everything
choices.why: Keeps philosophical contrast between seeming and being and Gregory’s claim that reason decides, not majority opinion.
rejected: for whom words matter more than life

choices.why: Marks repeated seeming versus being contrast; brief has no fixed gloss, so plain nouns keep negation and force.
Means insults suffered as public shame, matching opponent’s claim to be ashamed for Gregory, not Gregory insulting others.

choices.term: τὸ ἔνδον καὶ ἐν ἡμῖν αὐτοῖς δικαστήριον
choices.english: the court within and in ourselves
choices.why: Inner tribunal of conscience and God’s judgments, contrasted with acquittal by many accusers; keeps judicial force.

bible_refs.note: τῷ εἰδότι τὰ πάντα πρὶν γενέσεως αὐτῶν = ὁ εἰδὼς πάντα πρὶν γενέσεως αὐτῶν
τῷ πλάσσοντι καταμόνας τὰς καρδίας ἡμῶν, τῷ συνιέντι εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔργα ἡμῶν = ὁ πλάσας καταμόνας τὰς καρδίας αὐτῶν, ὁ συνιῶν εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶν
ἄνθρωπος εἰς πρόσωπον, ὁ δὲ Θεὸς εἰς καρδίαν = ἄνθρωπος ὄψεται εἰς πρόσωπον, ὁ δὲ Θεὸς ὄψεται εἰς καρδίαν

pass_b_english: But, my good fellow, if we offer a hand to a ship tossed by a storm, or to a city under siege, or to a house being eaten by fire — bringing help with skiffs, or with a battle line, or with fire engines — you would still call us either those who sink ships, or lovers of that city or that house, and never its protectors and guardians.

"But most people do not see it that way," my opponent says. What difference does that make to me, for whom reason counts for more than being, or rather for everything? For reason is what condemned or acquitted me, what made me wretched or blessed. Seeming is nothing to me, like another person's dream. "You do not look that way to most people, fellow," he says. Does the earth stand still to the dizzy? To drunkards, do sober men look sober, and not walking on their heads or spinning around? Is honey not bitter to the sick and disordered when they taste it? Yet things are not so because sufferers think them so. Show me, then, that those who suppose this about me are healthy, and then advise me to change. Or condemn me, if I refuse persuasion and still stand by the same judgment. I do not look this way to most people, but I do to God. I do not merely look so; I stand revealed before him who knows all things before they come to be (Susanna 42), who fashions our hearts, each one alone, who understands all our works (Psalm 33:15), our stirrings and our thoughts, with which our deeds are done, from whom nothing that is escapes notice and nothing can escape, who sees our affairs differently than men see them. For man looks to the face, but God looks to the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). You have heard Scripture saying this, so believe it. He is the one anyone with sense must care for above all others together. If you took counsel from two men about the same matter, one wise and one ignorant, would you be thought sensible if you passed over the wiser and followed the more ignorant? Rehoboam won no praise for dishonoring the counsel of the elders and setting up the counsel of the young. When God and men are weighed against each other, will you prefer what men think? You will not, if you listen to me and think better.

"But we are ashamed of you because of your disgraces," he says. And I am ashamed of you, because you are ashamed. For if I suffer these things justly, I have more reason to be ashamed for myself than you have to be ashamed for me — not because I am dishonored, but because I deserve dishonor. If I suffer them unjustly, the charge belongs to those who insult me, and you should be indignant for them rather than for me; they are the ones in a bad way. If I were bad and you supposed me excellent, what should I have done? Become worse, to please you more? I would never have given myself that advice. So too, if you suppose me stumbling when I am doing right, I will not abandon doing right for your sake. For I live not more for you than for myself. I take reason as my counselor in everything, and the judgments of God, by which I am often convicted when no one accuses me, and acquitted when many condemn me. There is only one thing no one can escape: the court within and in ourselves. We must look to it alone and walk the straight road.
notes: Print splits words with spaces from OCR: κηδε μόνας for κηδεμόνας, διακει μένοις, παραί νεσον, πειθο μένων, καρ δίας, γενέ σεως, δύ ναται; read as continuous forms without inventing text.

problems.quote: If you supposed me bad when I was excellent, what should I have done?
problems.source_quote: Εἰ δέ με ὄντα κακὸν, ἄριστον ὑπελάμβανες
problems.why: Reversed: the source says I was bad and you took me to be excellent. The English makes me excellent and you think me bad, which breaks the following 'become worse' logic.
problems.fix: But if I were bad and you supposed me excellent, what should I have done?

edits.old: If you supposed me bad when I was excellent, what should I have done?
edits.new: If I were bad and you supposed me excellent, what should I have done?

fixed: agency: real reversal fixed; source Ὀ δέ με ὄντα κακὸν, ἄριστον ὑπελάμβανες has me being bad and you supposing me excellent

problems.quote: Or condemn them, when they refuse persuasion and still stand by the same judgment.
problems.source_quote: ἢ καταγίνωσκε, μὴ πειθομένων, ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τῆς αὐτῆς ἱσταμένων κρίσεως.
problems.why: After “advise us,” the genitives are Gregory’s side: condemn us if we will not be moved, not the crowd.
problems.fix: Or else condemn me if I will not be persuaded and still stand by the same judgment.
problems.ruling: καταγίνωσκε takes a genitive object (μὴ πειθομένων… ἱσταμένων), meaning those not persuaded, i.e. Gregory's side after ἡμῖν. 'Condemn them' wrongly targets the crowd.

problems.quote: That is what anyone with sense must care for above all else together.
problems.source_quote: Οὗ φροντιστέον μᾶλλον, ἢ πάντων ὁμοῦ τῶν ἄλλων, τοῖς γε νοῦν ἔχουσιν.
problems.why: Οὗ refers to God, the one who sees the heart. The English turns it into an impersonal 'that' with no clear referent.
problems.fix: His opinion, above that of all others together, is the one that people with sense must care about.
problems.ruling: Masculine Οὗ resumes Θεός: care for him more than πάντων ὁμοῦ τῶν ἄλλων. Impersonal “that” loses the person.

edits.old: Or condemn them, when they refuse persuasion and still stand by the same judgment.
edits.new: Or condemn me, if I refuse persuasion and still stand by the same judgment.

edits.old: That is what anyone with sense must care for above all else together.
edits.new: He is the one anyone with sense must care for above all others together.

fixed: agency: changed crowd to Gregory — μὴ πειθομένων/ἱσταμένων follows ἡμῖν παραίνεσον μετατίθεσθαι and means Gregory refusing the advised change.
mistranslation: changed impersonal 'That' to God — Οὗ refers to Θεὸς who sees the heart, cared for μᾶλλον ἢ πάντων ὁμοῦ τῶν ἄλλων.
earlier edit stands, no change: με ὄντα κακὸν (reality bad) vs ἄριστον ὑπελάμβανες (supposed best) already matches 'If I were bad and you supposed me excellent'.

last_rejected.quote: for whom reason counts for more than being, or rather for everything? For reason is what condemned or acquitted me, what made me wretched or blessed.
last_rejected.source_quote: ᾧ τοῦ εἶναι πλεῖον ὁ λόγος, μᾶλλον δὲ πᾶς; Τοῦτο γὰρ, ἢ κατέκρινεν, ἢ ἐδικαίωσεν
last_rejected.why: The contrast is being versus seeming. ὁ λόγος means 'my concern', and Τοῦτο refers to actual being. English makes 'reason' the thing that condemns or acquits, and this loses the being/seeming contrast.
last_rejected.fix: What difference does it make to me, whose concern is mostly, or rather wholly, with what I am? For what I am either condemns or acquits me, makes me wretched or blessed.
last_rejected.ruling: πλεῖον τοῦ εἶναι is ‘more than being’; λόγος as reason is normal, and Τοῦτο resumes λόγος, which later counsels and judges.
